files.lesson.md: --- order: 1 unit: expressions node: AC9M7A01 n1 title: Letters that vary summary: In a formula, letters stand for quantities that can change (variables) and numbers stay the same (constants). In an equation, a letter can stand for one unknown number. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Recipes, phone bills and the perimeter of a garden bed all follow a formula. Some parts of a formula change from case to case and some never do. Which are which?" connection: ladder-points # data/connections/maths.yml (documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8142 url: http://127.0.0.1:8142/index.html readySelector: "#sl-l" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: formula.yml#pic, caption: "$P = 2l + 2w$: $P$, $l$ and $w$ are variables (each rectangle has its own); the 2s are constants (the same for every rectangle)." } explainClip: query: { code: "@formula.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Variables change; constants stay the same" say: "In a formula, the letters can change, and the numbers stay the same." clip: - caption: { text: "P = 2l + 2w: the perimeter of a rectangle.", say: "P equals two l plus two w: the perimeter of a rectangle." } - click: Make l bigger - click: Make l bigger - caption: { text: "Change l: the rectangle and P change.", say: "Change l, and the rectangle and its perimeter change too." } - click: Make w bigger - caption: { text: "Change w: P changes again. The 2s never do.", say: "Change w, and P changes again; the twos never change." } - caption: { text: "l, w and P are variables; the 2s are constants.", say: "So l, w and P are variables, and the twos are constants." } - expect: { selector: ".rulework", contains: "P = 2 × 6 + 2 × 3" } - wait: 1200 --- In maths a letter can stand for a number. A **formula** such as $P = 2l + 2w$ uses letters for quantities, here the perimeter $P$, length $l$ and width $w$ of a rectangle. So what do the letters and numbers in a formula each stand for, and which of them can change? ## Predict: what changes? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to which parts change exposes the idea that each letter stands for one fixed number." check: type: predict q: "$P = 2l + 2w$ gives the perimeter of a rectangle. When you draw a different rectangle, which parts of the formula change?" options: - "$l$, $w$ and $P$ change; the 2s stay the same" - "Only $P$ changes" - "Nothing: each letter stands for one fixed number" - "The 2s change as well" actual: "l, w and P change, because different rectangles have different lengths, widths and perimeters. The 2s stay the same for every rectangle: there are always two lengths and two widths." ``` $$P = 2l + 2w$$ Think of two different rectangles: a long thin one and a square. What is the same about how you find their perimeters? ## Run: change the rectangle ```step stage: run insight: "Moving l and w and watching P change, while the 2s never do, shows what a variable is." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#run", height: 520 } check: { type: board, text: "Make a rectangle 7 cm long and 2 cm wide. What is its perimeter?", when: "l = 7 and w = 2" } ``` Change $l$ and $w$. Watch the rectangle, the working and $P$. Which numbers in the formula never change? ## Investigate: variables, constants and unknowns ```step stage: investigate insight: "A variable is a letter for a quantity that can change; a constant stays the same; in an equation a letter can be an unknown, one particular number." tasks: - check: type: question q: "A plumber charges $C = 5h + 20$ dollars for a job of $h$ hours. Which are the variables?" options: ["$C$ and $h$", "5 and 20", "Only $h$"] answer: 0 explain: "C and h change from job to job. 5 (dollars an hour) and 20 (the call-out fee) are constants: the same for every job." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#kim" text: "Kim works out the perimeter. Click the line where her thinking goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: letter-alphabet explain: "Line 2: a letter stands for a quantity, here the length, not its place in the alphabet. l can be any length: you need to measure or be told it." - check: type: question q: "In the equation $3x + 2 = 14$, what does $x$ stand for?" options: ["An unknown: one number makes it true", "A variable that can be any number", "The letter x, not a number"] answer: 0 explain: "In an equation, the letter is an unknown: only x = 4 makes 3x + 2 = 14 true. In a formula, a letter is a variable that can take many values." ``` ### Reading a formula Here is how to read the parts of a formula. ```worked P = 2l + 2w :: The perimeter of a rectangle: twice the length plus twice the width. P, \; l, \; w :: These letters are **variables**: quantities that change from one rectangle to the next. 2 :: The 2s are **constants**: they are the same for every rectangle. l = 5, \; w = 3 :: For one particular rectangle, each variable has a value. 3x + 2 = 14 :: In an equation, a letter can be an **unknown**: one particular number. x = 4 :: Only one value makes this equation true. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Kim's working one line at a time. What does $l$ stand for? ### Unknown or variable? ## Modify: other formulas ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a formula with a constant added, one with a single variable, a product of two variables, and a letter that is a constant." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#plumber", height: 420 } tasks: - starter: "formula.yml#plumber" check: type: answer q: "In $C = 5h + 20$, what is the charge for a job of 0 hours (just the call-out)?" answer: "20" feedback: - ["25", "Put 0 in place of h: 5 × 0 = 0. What is left?"] - ["0", "The 20 is a constant: it is paid even when h is 0."] explain: "C = 5 × 0 + 20 = 20. The constant 20 is the call-out fee." - starter: "formula.yml#drive" check: type: question q: "A car travels at 60 km/h: $d = 60t$. Which part stays the same for the whole trip?" options: ["60, the speed", "$d$, the distance", "$t$, the time"] answer: 0 explain: "The speed 60 is a constant. The time t and the distance d both change as the trip goes on." - starter: "formula.yml#area" check: type: question q: "In $A = lw$ (the area of a rectangle), what happens to $A$ if $l$ doubles and $w$ stays the same?" options: ["$A$ doubles", "$A$ stays the same", "$A$ goes up by 2"] answer: 0 explain: "lw means l × w. Twice the length times the same width gives twice the area. Try it on the board." - check: type: question q: "The circumference of a circle is $C = \\pi d$. $\\pi$ is a letter. Is it a variable or a constant?" options: ["A constant: about 3.14 for every circle", "A variable: it changes with the circle", "An unknown we need to solve for"] answer: 0 explain: "π (pi) is a Greek letter for one particular number, about 3.14, the same for every circle. C and d are the variables." ``` ### A plumber Each task loads a new formula. Change the variables and watch what stays the same. ### A car trip ### Area ### A letter that never changes ## Practise: read the formula ```step stage: practise insight: "Naming variables, constants and unknowns, and saying what a constant means, in new formulas." tasks: - check: type: question q: "Water in a tank: $V = 3t + 10$ litres after $t$ minutes. What does the 10 mean?" options: ["10 litres in the tank at the start", "10 litres added every minute", "The tank fills in 10 minutes"] answer: 0 explain: "When t = 0, V = 10: the 10 litres were there at the start. 3 litres are added each minute." - check: type: question q: "Which letters are variables in $T = 12n + 6$ (the cost of $n$ concert tickets)?" options: ["$T$ and $n$", "12 and 6", "Only $T$"] answer: 0 explain: "T and n change with the order. 12 (dollars a ticket) and 6 (the booking fee) stay the same." - check: type: question q: "In $2y + 1 = 9$, what is $y$?" options: ["An unknown: $y = 4$ makes it true", "A variable: any value works", "A constant"] answer: 0 explain: "It is an equation, so y is an unknown: 2 × 4 + 1 = 9, and no other value works." ``` ### What the constant means ### Variables ### Unknown ## Make: a formula of your own ```step stage: make insight: "Writing a formula for a familiar shape reverses the lesson: from the quantities to the letters and constants." hint: ["A square has four equal sides, each s long.", "How many lots of s make the perimeter?"] check: type: answer q: "A square has sides of length $s$. Write a formula for its perimeter $P$. Start with $P =$." answer: "4s" feedback: - ["s + 4", "That adds 4 to one side. The perimeter is all four sides added up."] - ["2s", "That is two sides. A square has four."] explain: "P = 4s: four sides, each s long. 4 is a constant; P and s are variables." ``` Name the variables and the constant in your formula. Stretch: write a formula for the perimeter of a triangle with sides $a$, $b$ and $c$. ## Make: a ladder, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "On a competition ladder, wins, draws and points change from team to team, while the points for a win and a draw stay the same: the same split as in the rectangle formula, in a table students read every week." hint: ["Which parts of P = 3W + D are different for every team?", "Put W = 6 and D = 4 in, with the × sign."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A competition ladder gives points by $P = 3W + D$, where $W$ is a team's wins and $D$ its draws. The Emus have won 6 games and drawn 4 (made up for the task). How many points do they have?" steps: - ["$P$ is points, $W$ is wins, $D$ is draws", "each letter stands for a quantity"] - ["$W$, $D$ and $P$ change from team to team. The 3 (and the 1 hiding beside $D$) stay the same", "variables change, constants do not"] - ["$P = 3 \\times 6 + 4 = 18 + 4 = 22$", "$3W$ means $3 \\times W$: wins are worth 3 points each"] - ["Check: 6 wins at 3 points is 18, and 4 draws at 1 point is 4", "$18 + 4 = 22$"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Which part of $P = 3W + D$ is the same for every team?" options: - "The 3, the points for a win" - "$W$, the number of wins" - "$P$, the points" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Every team has its own number of wins. That one changes.", "Every team has its own points. That one changes."] answer: "22" tolerance: 0 answerLabel: "Points" feedback: - ["364", "$3W$ means $3 \\times W$, not 3 and 6 side by side."] - ["10", "That adds $W$ and $D$. A win is worth 3 points, not 1."] criteria: - "I named the variables and the constants." - "I wrote 3 × 6 with the × sign." - "I checked my answer with the points for wins and draws." explain: "Variables: $P$, $W$ and $D$. Constants: the 3 and the 1. $P = 3 \\times 6 + 4 = 22$ points." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The Emus' results are made up for the task, but the 3-and-1 rule is how many ladders work. Sort the letters into those that change and those that stay, then work out the points and type your answer. **Also used in** - **Ladders and scoreboards.** Wins and draws change from team to team, and the points for each stay the same. - **Spreadsheets and price lists.** Every total is a rule with slots: write it once, and it works for any case. - **Next lessons.** Putting numbers in, then the same letters in every formula in science and later maths. ```teacher summary: Students tell the variables in a formula from the constants, and see that in an equation a letter can be one unknown number (AC9M7A01, node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min struggle: Seeing that a letter stands for a quantity that can change, not one fixed number and not its place in the alphabet. Ask "what does this letter stand for, and what else could it be?" goals: - I can say which letters in a formula are variables and which numbers are constants. - I can say what a constant means in a real formula, such as a call-out fee. - I can tell a variable (can take many values) from an unknown (one value makes the equation true). before: > Do the Run board yourself first: change l and w and watch the working. The new move is reading a letter as a quantity that changes. Students often think each letter has one fixed value, or link a letter to its place in the alphabet (Kim's mistake). Keep saying the quantity aloud: "l, the length", not just "l". This lesson does not ask students to calculate much; the next lesson is substitution. The board does the arithmetic so attention stays on what changes. running: - "Predict: ask students who chose 'Nothing changes' to describe two different rectangles. Do they have the same length?" - "Run: before they reach l = 7, w = 2, ask: which numbers in the working never changed?" - "Investigate: model the worked example live. Draw the contrast on the board: formula (variables, many values) and equation (unknown, one value)." - "Modify: for π, point out that a letter is not automatically a variable." - "Make: have two students compare 4s with s + s + s + s. Are they the same formula?" - "Paper: the ladder task is worked in books; the page marks the points (22) and the reason the 3 is a constant. Books out, and look for the letters sorted into changes and stays the same before any arithmetic." stuck: - see: A student gives a letter its alphabet value (Kim's mistake). ask: What does l stand for in this formula? How would you find its value? fix: A letter stands for a quantity. Its value is measured or given, and can change from one rectangle to the next. - see: A student says the 2 in 2l is a variable because it is next to a letter. ask: Draw a different rectangle. Did the 2 change? fix: "Constants stay the same for every case. 2l means 2 × l: two lengths." stretch: Write a formula for the cost of n pizzas at 15 dollars each with a 5 dollar delivery fee. Name every variable and constant, and say what each constant means. support: Give a two-column table, 'changes' and 'stays the same', to sort the parts of each formula into before answering. leads: > Next: substituting into formulas, then finding an unknown in a formula. Later, linear relations use the same letters: in y = mx + c, x and y vary and m and c are constants for one line. exit: q: A taxi charges T = 2d + 4 dollars for d km. Name the variables and the constants, and say what the 4 means. a: "Variables: T and d. Constants: 2 and 4. The 4 is the fee to get in, paid even for 0 km." explain: > In a **formula**, letters stand for quantities. A letter whose value can change is a **variable**; a number that stays the same is a **constant**. In $P = 2l + 2w$, $P$, $l$ and $w$ are variables and the 2s are constants. In an **equation** such as $3x + 2 = 14$, the letter is an **unknown**: one particular number ($x = 4$) makes it true. ```
